name: Multi-LLM Chat
tag: Ask once and see how several AI models answer, side by side, so you can pick the best one.

scenarios.title: Compare answers on a contract question
scenarios.ask: Send one prompt about a {words}-word supplier contract to {models} AI models and show where they agree, with {priority} as the tie-breaker.
steps: Router
Sent the same prompt and contract text to {models} models at once, about {=round(words * 1.33)} tokens each.
Collector
Gathered all answers. The fastest came back in about {=round(2 + words / 1500, 1)} seconds, the slowest in {=round(4 + words / 600, 1)}.
Comparer
Lined up the answers clause by clause. All models agreed on {=max(3, 9 - models)} key terms.
Difference finder
Flagged {=models - 1} points where answers differ, such as the notice period for termination.
Picker
Ranked the answers using {priority} as the tie-breaker and marked the strongest one.

result.title: Side-by-side result
rows: Check flagged points against the contract itself

followups: Different models read long text differently and some skip details near the end. A disagreement is a signal to read that clause yourself, which is often the most useful thing the comparison gives you.
Is my contract sent anywhere else?
Only to the model providers you switch on. You can turn off any provider, and the chat history stays in your workspace.
Do I always need this many models?
No. Many teams use two for everyday questions and add more only for high-stakes text like contracts.

scenarios.title: Pick a default model for the team
scenarios.ask: Our team sends about {prompts} prompts a month. Compare {models} models on our typical questions and pick a default.
steps: Sampler
Pulled 50 recent prompts and grouped them: {=simple}% simple, {=100 - simple}% complex.
Router
Ran all 50 prompts on {models} models and saved the answers side by side.
Reviewer
Asked two team members to score blind answers. Scores were within 10% on simple questions.
Planner
Suggested a lower-cost model for simple questions and a stronger model for the rest.

result.title: Model plan
rows: Cost if everything used the stronger model

followups: How was the price per prompt worked out?
This demo uses sample rates of 0.2 cents for a simple prompt and 2 cents for a complex one. In your workspace it uses your real provider prices and token counts.
Can people still pick a model themselves?
Yes. The default is just a starting point. Anyone can open the side-by-side view and choose a different answer.

scenarios.title: Check a fact before publishing
scenarios.ask: Before we publish a blog post, check {claims} factual claims by asking {models} models and flag any where they disagree.
steps: Extractor
Pulled {claims} factual claims out of the draft, such as dates, numbers and definitions.
Router
Asked {models} models to check each claim and say how sure they are.
Comparer
{=max(0, claims - ceil(claims * 0.2))} claims had matching answers. {=ceil(claims * 0.2)} had mixed answers.
Editor
Listed the mixed claims with a note to check a primary source before publishing.
followups: If all models agree, is the claim true?
Not necessarily. Models can share the same wrong information. Agreement lowers the risk, but a primary source is still the real check for anything important.
Models that support web search can return links, and the chat shows them next to each answer so you can open and verify them.
